newsitem.title: UK: ICCO group meets to step up accuracy in stocks.
newsitem.headline: ICCO group meets to step up accuracy in stocks.

text.p: A group of cocoa traders and analysts were meeting under the umbrella of the International Cocoa Organisation (ICCO) on Thursday with a view to improve the accuracy of stocks data, delegates at a conference said.
Discussions are likely to focus on the ICCO stock figure for the season ended September 1996 of 1.4 million tonnes which some members said was overestimated and must be revised down.
Controversy stemmed from a wide gap between the estimates of the ICCO and the UK-based trade and research group E.D.& F Man which pegged the stocks at 1.09 million in September.
Another UK cocoa researcher, PCR Ltd, estimated the 1995/96 stocks at 1.2 million tonnes.
"1.4 million is too high. It should be just below 1.3 million," said the head of the trade association of one consumer country who did not want to be named.
An ICCO working group on stocks will assess the volume, location and the composition of stocks and urge reluctant members to contribute more data.

This may be tricky as some do not want to provide what they see as commercially-sensitive information. The ICCO's latest calculations released in October put stocks in importing countries at 1.044 million. Factory stocks derived from grindings in importing countries were at 106,000 tonnes and stocks in producing countries were 70,000 tonnes.
A total 90,000 tonnes of cocoa beans were classified as beans in transit from producing to consuming countries.

Traders said the inconsistency in figures could be due to the assumption made to gauge the size of unallocated cocoa which the ICCO put at 94,000 tonnes for 1995/96. There could also be a risk of error of double counting of manufacturer or warehouse stocks, they said.
"It is quite possible that the ICCO may revise its 1995/96 figure," said Tim Mordan, UK delegate and the chairman of the executive board.
A possible change in the way stocks are calculated would also be reflected in upcoming estimates for 1996/97, he said.
Achieving accuracy in stocks is crucial for the ICCO to implement a production management plan which envisages worldwide cuts based on a ratio of stocks to consumption of 34 percent.
Producers have been asked to curb output by 90,000 tonnes in the next three years to bring the ratio down from about 50 percent now as a result of record West African harvests.
"You need to have the right basis. If your stock figure is wrong, you won't be able to implement the production cuts properly," said the delegate who wanted to remain unanimous.
The ICCO estimated stocks in Western European ports and warehouses, excluding the ICCO buffer stocks at 592,000 tonnes.
The only estimate for 1996/97 so far came from PCR who pegged it at 1.078 tonnes.
